full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN-VARIANT.** The closest published system uses disks. The rule system here uses slightly elongated particles with orientation-dependent interactions.

**1. Model family.** This is chiral or odd active matter. Overdamped Brownian particles interact through a conservative Lennard-Jones potential plus a pairwise non-conservative transverse (odd) force. The transverse force has no radial component and always has the same rotational sense. It is the "chiral Lennard-Jones fluid" or "odd crystal" setting, studied in 2D with defect and hexatic-order diagnostics.

**2. Specific behaviour.**
- **What the run shows.** With e_a/e_p = 33, the transverse force is far stronger than the conservative one. A starting crystal at density about 0.87 loses its six-fold order and produces many defects. Density becomes very uneven (density CV 0.43). Polar order is near zero (0.04) and local alignment is near zero (−0.036). The nearest-neighbour ratio of 1.975 is well above 1, so there is no clumping in the clustering sense. I read these numbers as describing a driven fluid with large density fluctuations, not an aligned or flocking state. The input doesn't define the metrics, so this is my interpretation.
- **Earliest clear source.** Braverman, Scheibner, VanSaders and Vitelli, "Topological Defects in Solids with Odd Elasticity", Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 268001 (2021). Odd elastic moduli modify defect-induced strain and can reverse the stability of bound dislocation pairs. Isolated dislocations can self-propel through microscopic work cycles at their cores. The paper's molecular-dynamics simulations used a Lennard-Jones radial force plus transverse forces. It reports that introducing transverse forces generally lowers the plastic yield. The snippet cuts off there, so I haven't seen the rest of that sentence.
- **Closest match.** Caporusso et al., "Phase Coexistence and Edge Currents in the Chiral Lennard-Jones Fluid", Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 168201 (2024). It studies Brownian disks interacting via a Lennard-Jones potential and a nonconservative transverse force. It reports that chirality can also break the solid phase, giving rise to a dense fluid made of rotating hexatic patches. This is the same rule structure with isotropic particles.
- **Related melting work.** "Melting of nonreciprocal solids: How dislocations propel and fission in flowing crystals" (PNAS, 2025) treats odd (transverse) forces as a separate case from nonreciprocal ones. It says odd forces produce a net simple shear on a dislocation and cause its gliding. A "dislocation proliferation then fragmentation of the crystal" picture appears there too. The search result has no author list, so I haven't verified the authors.
- **Review.** Grain boundaries glide over one another and individually rotating domains "knead" the odd crystal. This comes from "Emergent phenomena in chiral active matter" (Nat. Sci. Open, 2024), which I saw only as a search snippet. Fruchart, Scheibner and Vitelli, "Odd Viscosity and Odd Elasticity", Annu. Rev. Condens. Matter Phys. 14, 471 (2023), is also a relevant review. It was confirmed only as a listed publication, and I didn't read it.

**3. What differs, and whether it matters.**
- **Particle shape.** The particles here are weakly elliptical (half-axes 0.55 and 0.65), with Gay-Berne-like orientation-dependent interactions and rotating orientations. The published work uses isotropic disks. I found no paper on chiral transverse-force Lennard-Jones fluids with elliptical particles.
- **Likely effect.** At aspect ratio about 1.18, the shape anisotropy is small, and orientations relax quickly. I expect it to change quantitative details such as thresholds, not the qualitative melting into a defected, density-heterogeneous chiral fluid.
- **Parameters.** The values e_a/e_p = 33 and T = 6 are probably deep in the melted regime, so this is not a boundary case. I haven't checked the exact thresholds in the papers.

**4. Confidence: medium.** The mechanism and the observable signatures (hexatic breakdown, defect proliferation, rotating hexatic patches, density inhomogeneity) are well covered for disks. The ellipse variant is a short, targeted gap, and I ran only about six searches, so a paper on anisotropic chiral particles could exist. I didn't read the full text of any of these papers. The six metrics (nn_ratio, density_cv, polar order and so on) have no clear counterpart in the literature, so I matched on behaviour, not numbers.
